description: The current account of the balance of payments, why deficits arise, and how income is distributed across society.
content_html:
The Balance of Payments

Every time the UK buys a foreign car or sells a software licence abroad, a record is made. The balance of payments is the account that tracks all money flowing into and out of the UK economy. The most important section for GCSE Economics is the current account, which covers trade in goods and services as well as investment income flowing in or out of the country.

The UK buys goods and services from other countries — these are imports. It also sells goods and services abroad — these are exports. When you subtract the value of imports from the value of exports, you get the balance of trade. If exports are greater than imports, there is a trade surplus; if imports exceed exports, there is a trade deficit.

Key Fact

A current account surplus means money flows into the country because exports exceed imports. A current account deficit means money flows out because imports exceed exports. The UK has run a current account deficit for most of the past four decades.

Why Do Surpluses and Deficits Arise?

A current account deficit can arise for a number of reasons. First, if consumer spending is high, households tend to buy more imports — trainers made overseas, electronics assembled abroad, food sourced internationally. Second, if domestic firms are relatively uncompetitive — perhaps because their costs are higher than foreign rivals — overseas products become more attractive to buyers at home and abroad. Third, a strong exchange rate makes UK exports more expensive for foreign buyers and imports cheaper for UK consumers, both of which worsen the current account.

A current account surplus tends to arise when a country produces things the world wants to buy. Countries like Germany have sustained surpluses because their manufacturers export high-value engineering goods in strong demand worldwide.

A persistent deficit has real costs. If the UK consistently spends more on imports than it earns from exports, it must borrow money from abroad or attract investment to cover the shortfall. Over time this can weaken the value of the pound — because more pounds are being sold to buy foreign currency to pay for imports — and it can make the country dependent on foreign creditors. Firms that produce goods facing strong import competition may cut jobs or close entirely.

However, a deficit is not necessarily a crisis. A growing economy naturally sucks in imports. If the deficit is financed by foreign investors buying UK assets and businesses because they believe in the UK’s long-term prospects, that is a sign of confidence. The key question is whether the deficit is sustainable — can it be financed without causing a damaging fall in the exchange rate or a rise in borrowing costs?

Government Policies to Influence the Current Account

Governments have several tools to try to reduce a current account deficit. They can use supply-side policies to make domestic firms more competitive — investing in education and training so workers are more skilled, or funding infrastructure to lower firms’ costs. A more competitive domestic industry exports more and is less undercut by imports. They can also allow the exchange rate to fall, making exports cheaper for foreign buyers and imports dearer for domestic consumers, though this tends to raise inflation. Import controls such as tariffs or quotas can limit imports directly, but these may provoke retaliation from trading partners.

Key Fact

Current account balance = Exports − Imports (plus net income flows and transfers). A positive value is a surplus; a negative value is a deficit. Performing simple calculations using current account figures is an assessed quantitative skill — always check whether the figure is positive (surplus) or negative (deficit).

The Distribution of Income

The distribution of income describes how earnings are divided across households. In the UK, as in most market economies, income is not shared equally. Some people earn much more than others because of differences in skills, qualifications, the type of work they do, and whether they own assets that generate income such as property or shares.

It is important to distinguish between income and wealth. Income is the flow of money a person receives over a period — wages, rent, profits and interest. Wealth is the stock of assets someone has built up over time. A person can have a high income but little wealth (for example, a well-paid worker who spends everything), or modest income but significant wealth (for example, someone who inherited property). Wealth inequality tends to be even more pronounced than income inequality.

Several factors drive the gap between higher and lower earners. Education and skills raise productivity and therefore wages — a software engineer earns more than an unskilled labourer partly because their skills are scarce and highly valued by firms. Inheritance means some households start with a significant asset base, allowing them to generate investment income that widens the gap over time. Market power of firms can hold wages down at the bottom of the labour market if workers have few alternatives.

Structural changes in the economy also play a role. Deindustrialisation reduced well-paid manual jobs in regions like the Midlands and North of England, leaving pockets of unemployment and lower earnings that persist across generations.

Consequences of Inequality

Inequality has consequences for individuals and for the economy as a whole. At the individual level, people on low incomes may struggle to afford adequate housing, food and healthcare. Children from poorer households may have less access to private tutoring and extracurricular activities, which can limit their future earnings — a cycle that can repeat across generations. From a macroeconomic perspective, very high inequality may reduce consumer spending overall if those at the top save most of their income rather than spend it, holding back demand.

On the other hand, some degree of inequality provides incentives. Higher rewards for skilled work or successful entrepreneurship encourage people to invest in their own education and training, which can raise the overall productivity of the economy. The debate over how much inequality is acceptable involves judgements about fairness and efficiency that go beyond economics alone.

The main tools of redistribution are taxation and government spending. A progressive tax such as income tax takes a bigger percentage from high earners than from low earners. This narrows the gap between gross (before-tax) and net (after-tax) incomes. The additional revenue can be spent on transfer payments — benefits such as Universal Credit, housing benefit and child benefit — which boost the incomes of lower-earning households.

The government can also reduce wealth inequality through inheritance tax, which taxes large transfers of wealth between generations, and by providing public services such as the NHS and state education that all households can access regardless of income. However, critics argue that very high tax rates can reduce incentives and may cause high earners to move abroad.

Linking the Two Objectives

The balance of payments and the distribution of income are both government objectives that can come into conflict with other goals. Reducing a current account deficit may require lower consumer spending, which could slow economic growth and raise unemployment. Redistributing income through higher taxes may reduce incentives to work or invest, potentially affecting productivity and long-run economic growth. Effective policy requires balancing these tensions — a judgement at the heart of many GCSE Economics evaluation questions.
exam_tip_html: When you see the command word Calculate, always show your working clearly — write the formula, substitute the numbers and state the sign of the answer (positive = surplus, negative = deficit). For Explain questions on income distribution, build a chain of reasoning: higher tax → more revenue → higher transfer payments → lower-income households receive more → gap between rich and poor narrows. For the Evaluate capstone, remember to analyse both sides and write a supported judgement using “it depends on…” — for example, whether a current account deficit is a problem depends on how it is being financed and the state of the wider economy.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The current account of the balance of payments records trade in goods and services. A deficit means imports exceed exports; a surplus means the reverse. Persistent deficits may require borrowing from abroad and can weaken the exchange rate.
  • Income and wealth are distributed unequally across society. Causes include differences in skills, inheritance and structural change in the economy. Inequality affects individuals through living standards and the broader economy through demand and incentives.
  • Governments redistribute income through progressive taxation and transfer payments, and reduce wealth inequality through public services and inheritance tax. These tools must be balanced against the risk of reducing incentives to work and invest.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a current account deficit?
A) A country’s exports are greater than its imports
B) A country’s imports are greater than its exports
C) A country’s government spending is greater than its tax revenue
D) A country’s savings are greater than its investment
practice_questions.marks: B) A country's imports are greater than its exports [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: In a given year, a country exports goods and services worth £480 billion and imports goods and services worth £530 billion. Calculate the current account balance and state whether it is a surplus or a deficit.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the correct method/formula: current account balance = exports minus imports (£480bn − £530bn); 1 mark for the correct answer of −£50 billion (a deficit).

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a country might have a persistent current account deficit.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a cause, for example: strong consumer spending or lack of domestic competitiveness or a high exchange rate; 1 mark for developing the point (e.g. high consumer spending raises demand for imported goods); 1 mark for a further development explaining the link to the current account (e.g. this means spending on imports rises, so imports exceed exports, worsening the deficit).

practice_questions.text: A government is concerned about a widening current account deficit. Using an example, explain how supply-side policies might help to reduce this deficit.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant supply-side policy (e.g. investment in education and training, or infrastructure spending); 1 mark for explaining how it improves competitiveness of domestic firms (e.g. better-skilled workers raise productivity, lowering unit costs); 1 mark for linking this to exports (e.g. lower costs allow UK firms to sell goods at more competitive prices abroad, so exports rise); 1 mark for linking to the current account (e.g. as exports rise relative to imports, the deficit narrows).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the use of progressive taxation and transfer payments can reduce income inequality in an economy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, connected analysis showing how progressive tax raises revenue (higher earners pay a larger proportion), which funds transfer payments that directly raise incomes at the bottom, narrowing the gap. Considers at least one limiting factor (e.g. disincentive effects, means-testing costs) and links to overall living standards or aggregate demand. Well-structured throughout.

Secure: Clear explanation of how progressive tax works and how transfer payments benefit lower-income households. Makes a reasonable connection between the two mechanisms. Limited treatment of any complications or counterpoints.

Developing: Identifies progressive taxation and transfer payments as tools. Explanation is partial — may describe one tool well but not link it clearly to reduced inequality, or chain of reasoning breaks.

Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points. May confuse progressive and regressive tax, or fail to explain how redistribution reduces the gap between rich and poor.

practice_questions.text:
'Reducing income inequality should always be the government's top economic priority.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• High inequality can reduce social mobility, as poorer households cannot invest in their children's education, locking in disadvantage across generations — a market economy alone will not correct this.
• Redistributing income towards lower earners may boost consumer spending, since lower earners spend a higher proportion of income (higher marginal propensity to consume), potentially supporting economic growth.
• Reducing poverty through transfer payments lowers social costs such as health spending and crime, benefiting the whole economy.

Arguments against:
• Prioritising redistribution may conflict with economic growth — very high income tax rates could reduce incentives to work and invest, shrinking the tax base over time.
• Reducing a current account deficit or controlling inflation may be more urgent priorities in certain conditions (e.g. high inflation erodes living standards for everyone).
• Some inequality is an incentive mechanism: the prospect of higher earnings encourages skill development and entrepreneurship, raising long-run productivity.

Judgement: The priority attached to reducing inequality depends on the severity of the inequality, the state of the economy (during a recession, growth and employment may be more pressing), and the values of the government in power. A balanced evaluation recognises that all government objectives are interconnected — policies that reduce inequality can support growth if they raise the productive capacity of the workforce, but can hinder it if they weaken incentives excessively.

Mastering: Both sides developed with chains of reasoning; explicitly links inequality reduction to other objectives (growth, employment); reaches a supported, conditional judgement using 'it depends on…' with clear criteria.

Secure: Both sides covered with explanation; reasonable conclusion, though judgement may not be fully supported with criteria.

Developing: Arguments on both sides listed but not well developed; conclusion present but not justified.

Emerging: One-sided or very brief points; no clear conclusion.

knowledge_checks.q: What does a current account deficit mean?
options: A country's exports are worth more than its imports
A country's government spends more than it collects in tax
A country's imports are worth more than its exports
A country's savings are greater than its investment

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an example of a progressive tax?
options: VAT, which is charged at a flat 20% on all goods and services
A council tax that is the same for every household
Income tax where higher earners pay a larger proportion
A flat fuel duty applied equally to all litres of petrol

knowledge_checks.q: The current account balance equals exports _____ imports.
_____ is the total value of assets a person owns, minus any debts, whereas income is the flow of money received over a period.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Exports exceed imports, so money flows into the country
A benefit paid by the government to boost lower household incomes
A tax where the rate rises as income increases

flashcard_questions.q: What does the balance of payments record?
flashcard_questions.a: All financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world over a year.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the current account of the balance of payments?
flashcard_questions.a: The section recording trade in goods and services, plus income flows and transfers.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a current account deficit indicate?
flashcard_questions.a: Imports exceed exports, so money flows out of the economy.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one reason why strong consumer spending can worsen a current account deficit.
flashcard_questions.a: Higher spending raises demand for imports, so import values rise relative to exports.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between income and wealth?
flashcard_questions.a: Income is the flow of money received over time; wealth is the stock of assets owned.
A tax where the rate rises as the taxable amount rises, so higher earners pay a larger proportion.

flashcard_questions.q: How do transfer payments help reduce income inequality?
flashcard_questions.a: They boost incomes of lower-earning households, narrowing the gap between rich and poor.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one long-run consequence of persistent income inequality for social mobility.
flashcard_questions.a: Poorer children may have less access to education, limiting future earnings across generations.
A long-term shift away from manufacturing towards service industries in an advanced economy.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a current account deficit require borrowing from abroad?
flashcard_questions.a: The shortfall between exports and imports must be financed by attracting foreign capital or credit.

flashcard_questions.q: How can supply-side policies help reduce a current account deficit?
flashcard_questions.a: By raising domestic competitiveness, firms export more and are less undercut by imports.

flashcard_questions.q: Which policy tool taxes large transfers of wealth between generations to reduce wealth inequality?

glossary_terms.definition: A record of all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world over a year.
The part of the balance of payments that records trade in goods and services, plus income flows and transfers.
When a country's imports of goods and services are greater than its exports, so money flows out of the economy.
How the total income of a country is shared out among its population.
The total value of assets a person owns, including property, savings and investments, minus any debts.
A long-term shift away from manufacturing towards service industries in an advanced economy.
A tax where the rate increases as the taxable amount increases, so higher earners pay a larger proportion of their income.
